newsitem.title: USA: Clinton threatens veto on flood aid bill.
newsitem.headline: Clinton threatens veto on flood aid bill.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton Monday threatened to veto an emergency flood relief bill for portions of the Midwest if Congress used it to attach conditions to budget talks.

Leaving on a visit to Mexico, Clinton was asked if he intended to carry out his threat to veto the bill if budget conditions were added. "I have no reason to change the position I outlined," he replied.
When it was pointed out that a veto would keep $5.5 billion in disaster relief from flowing to victims, Clinton replied: "That's right, that's why Congress ought to pass it unemcumbered."

Republicans used the emergency relief bill to attach a provision that would prevent any shutdown of the federal government this fall if Congress and the White House do not agree on a budget for the next fiscal year.
The White House objects to the provision, saying it would undercut budget negotiations by removing the need for both sides to make compromises.
Although Clinton and the Republican-controlled Congress agreed on a budget outline last week to balance the budget by 2002, the two sides face difficult negotiations on details of implementation.
Republican efforts to force Clinton to cut government spending to balance the federal budget shut down most of the U.S. government twice, in late 1995 and early 1996.

The Senate began debate on the flood relief bill Monday and former Senate Democratic Leader Robert Byrd accused Republicans of trying to embarrass Clinton by forcing him to veto aid for disaster victims.

"The only conclusion I can reach is that the (Republican) majority has somehow calculated that they can win the public relations battle on these controversial riders and place the blame on the president when he vetoes the bill," Byrd said.
"Meanwhile, the hundreds of thousands of victims in 33 states who are suffering from the ravages of the disasters which this bill addresses will have to wait," the West Virginia Democrat said.

The provision added to the flood relief bill by Republican leaders is called the "Government Shutdown Prevention Act" and would specify that if disputes on funding of major programmes cannot be worked out this year the programmes will continue at 98 percent of the present rate.
